segments.english: From the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat from it; for on the day you eat from it you shall surely die.
segments.literal: and-from tree of-the-knowledge good and-evil not you-shall-eat from-it; for in-day of-your-eating from-it dying you-shall-die

tokens.note: the ו is conjunctive and is not rendered in the English

The pack gives the lemma key bdb:i.ai.ac (the noun entry, 'a good thing') with parse adjective; the adjective entry is bdb:i.ai.ab. The data is kept. Sense 4, moral good, is the noun-entry sense that fits 'good and evil'.
second-person yiqtol after לֹא: a prohibition
infinitive construct with the suffix ךָ: 'in the day of your eating'
infinitive absolute, emphatic

phrases.english: From the tree of the knowledge of good and evil
phrases.literal: 'and-from tree of-the-knowledge good and-evil': a construct chain (tree of knowledge), with good and evil as one pair
'not you-shall-eat': a prohibition in the second-person yiqtol
'from-it': the pronoun repeats the first clause. Ibn Ezra reads it as explanatory; Ramban reads it as 'from its fruit'
'for': the כִּי opens the consequence clause
'in-day of-your-eating': a temporal clause. 'On the day' is kept; its timing is disputed (see note)
'from-it'
'dying you-shall-die': infinitive absolute and finite verb of one root, emphatic

grammar: לֹא תֹאכַל is a prohibition: a second-person yiqtol after לֹא, so 'you shall not eat'.
The etnaḥta on מִמֶּנּוּ (2:17.7) divides the verse: the prohibition first, then the consequence that begins with כִּי.
מוֹת תָּמוּת is an infinitive absolute followed by a yiqtol of the same root, giving emphasis: 'you shall surely die'.
בְּיוֹם אֲכָלְךָ: the infinitive construct with the suffix ךָ gives 'your eating'; the preposition בְּ makes it a time clause, 'on the day you eat'.
מִמֶּנּוּ appears twice. The English keeps 'from it' both times, and the apparatus records the commentators' readings of the pronoun.
segments.note: 'On the day' (בְּיוֹם): Ramban takes it as 'at the time you eat', with death as liability from that moment and the death itself later (Gen 3:19). The English keeps the phrase and does not decide the timing.

commentary.summary: Ibn Ezra asks why 'from it' is needed after 'you shall not eat from it'. He gives two answers: it is an explanatory addition, as in 'and she opened it and saw him, the child' (Exod 2:6), or it means 'even a little of it'. The English follows the first, with no added 'even a little'; the second is recorded in the apparatus.
Ramban (not normative): 'from it' warns against eating from its fruit, since the tree itself is not eaten. The English keeps 'it' and does not name the fruit.

Ramban (not normative): 'on the day you eat ... you shall surely die' means that at the moment of eating you become liable to death, not that you die that day. Recorded; the English keeps the timing open.

apparatus: Ibn Ezra's second reading of מִמֶּנּוּ, 'even a little of it', is not adopted in the English.
Ramban's reading of 'on the day' as 'at the moment' is recorded, not adopted.

segments.english: The LORD God said: 'It is not good for the human to be alone; I will make for him a helper corresponding to him.'
segments.literal: and-said the-LORD God not-good to-be the-human alone; I-will-make for-him a-helper like-in-front-of-him

tokens.note: wayyiqtol: the verb comes before its subject
plural form with a singular verb; the name of the God of Israel, rendered 'God' by the decision
predicate of a verbless clause: 'is not good'
infinitive construct as subject: 'the being of the human alone'
לְ + בַד + וֹ: 'by itself'
first-person yiqtol in the LORD's speech. The WLC form differs (apparatus).
dative: 'for him'
one who helps; Ibn Ezra compares 'two are better than one' (Eccl 4:9)
כְּ + נֶגֶד + וֹ, 'like what is in front of him'. The English keeps the ambiguity; see commentary.

phrases.literal: 'and-said the-LORD God': the verb comes first in the wayyiqtol; the English puts the subject first

phrases.english: it is not good for the human to be alone
phrases.literal: 'not-good to-be the-human alone': a verbless clause whose subject is the infinitive; 'it is' is supplied

phrases.english: I will make for him a helper corresponding to him
phrases.literal: 'I-will-make for-him a-helper like-in-front-of-him': 'corresponding to him' keeps the crux of כְּנֶגְדּוֹ

grammar: לֹא־טוֹב הֱיוֹת הָאָדָם לְבַדּוֹ has no finite verb. The infinitive הֱיוֹת is its subject, so the English supplies 'it is'.
וַיֹּאמֶר is a wayyiqtol, so the verb comes first; the English moves the subject ahead of it.
The etnaḥta on לְבַדּוֹ (2:18.8) divides the divine judgment from the intention that follows.
אֶעֱשֶׂה־לּוֹ עֵזֶר: a first-person yiqtol with the dative לוֹ before the object עֵזֶר. The English keeps that order: 'I will make for him a helper'.
כְּנֶגְדּוֹ is the crux. 'In front of him' gives both 'corresponding to him' and 'against him'. Rashi's second reading ('against him, to fight') is recorded in the commentary.
segments.note: 'Corresponding to him' keeps the ambiguity of כְּנֶגְדּוֹ. Ibn Ezra, Radak and Sforno read the word as a counterpart standing before him, or as an equal; the English does not render 'against him'.

commentary.summary: Rashi: 'not good' is said so that no one thinks there are two powers, the Holy One alone above without a mate and this one alone below without a mate (Bereshit Rabbah). The English keeps the plain 'not good ... alone'; the reason is given here, not in the English.

Rashi: 'if he merits, a helper; if not, "against him" to fight' (Bereshit Rabbah). The English keeps 'corresponding to him', so the ambiguity stays open. Rashi's second reading is recorded in the apparatus and not adopted.
Ibn Ezra gives the sense of 'not good' as 'not good for the human' (לְאָדָם): the judgment concerns the human's situation. The English reads 'it is not good for the human to be alone'.
Ibn Ezra explains 'a helper' by 'two are better than one' (Eccl 4:9): the helper is one who gives help, as in 'a helper'.

Ramban (not normative): in creation 'good' means permanence (הַקִּיּוּם); a man alone would not endure, so 'not good' means he would not last alone, and the helper is for bearing seed. The English uses 'good' in the sense of 'not good for', not permanence; recorded here.

Sforno (not normative): כְּנֶגְדּוֹ is the image of a balance, two pans set opposite each other, equal in weight but not identical. The English 'corresponding to him' follows this picture of an equal counterpart.

apparatus: 2:18.9 (אֶֽעֱשֶׂה): the WLC reads אֶֽעֱשֶׂהּ; the pack keeps the base form אֶֽעֱשֶׂה.
2:18.10 (לּוֹ): the pack's WLC note says the BHS form is kept where the form's validity is in question.
2:18.12 (כְּנֶגְדּוֹ): Rashi's second reading, 'against him, to fight', is recorded and not adopted.

segments.english: Now the LORD God formed from the ground every wild animal of the field and every bird of the sky, and brought them to the human to see what he would call it; and whatever the human called each living creature, that is its name.
segments.literal: and-formed the-LORD God from the-ground all wild-animals-of the-field and-[obj] all birds-of the-sky, and-brought to the-human to-see what he-would-call to-it; and-all which he-would-call to-it the-human living-creature, that is-its-name

tokens.note: wayyiqtol; divine activity. Rashi: the same formation as above, not a new act
Rashi: 'from the ground' is also said of the birds, which came from the rekek (Chullin 27b)
construct chain, 'beast of the field', as a collective
וְ + the object marker אֵת, which introduces a second object: the birds
hifil: bring near
infinitive construct of purpose
interrogative
yiqtol after מַה: 'what he would call'
לוֹ: the dative, 'to it': name it. The suffix is masculine singular for each creature.
free relative with כֹּל: 'and whatever'
relative particle
dative, as at 2:19.19
נֶפֶשׁ: 'a living being'. Rashi and Ibn Ezra take it as the object of the calling.
adjective in apposition
הוּא, 'it is'

phrases.english: the LORD God formed from the ground
phrases.literal: 'and-formed the-LORD God from the-ground': the verb comes first; Rashi reads the formation as the one described above

phrases.english: every wild animal of the field
phrases.literal: 'all wild-animals-of the-field': the construct chain 'beast of the field'

phrases.english: and every bird of the sky
phrases.literal: 'and-[obj] all birds-of the-sky': the object marker introduces the second object

phrases.english: and brought them to the human
phrases.literal: 'and-brought to the-human': no object is written; 'them' is supplied

phrases.english: to see what he would call it
phrases.literal: 'to-see what he-would-call to-it': the purpose clause, with the modal yiqtol
'and-all which he-would-call to-it the-human': the free relative clause; the English places 'the human' before 'called'
'living-creature living': the object of the calling, in apposition
'that is-its-name': the name is the predicate

grammar: The wayyiqtol chain 'formed ... and brought' is narrative. Radak reads the first verb as a pluperfect; the English uses the simple past.
לִרְאוֹת מַה־יִּקְרָא־לוֹ: the infinitive of purpose, then an interrogative with a yiqtol: 'to see what he would call it'.
וְכֹל אֲשֶׁר יִקְרָא־לוֹ: a free relative. The noun נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה stands in apposition, and 'that is its name' has הוּא as the subject pronoun.
The etnaḥta on לוֹ (2:19.19) divides the verse into the bringing and the naming.
The lamed of לוֹ in the relative clause can take נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה with it. Rashi and Ibn Ezra both take it as the object of the calling, so the English reads 'called each living creature'.
segments.note: 'Formed' (2:19.1): Rashi reads it as the same act already described, so the English uses the simple past. Radak's pluperfect is recorded in the commentary.

commentary.summary: Rashi: the formation is the one mentioned above, not a new act. 'From the ground' also covers the birds, which Rashi takes from the rekek and not from the waters of 1:20. The animals were brought to Adam on the day they were formed. The English follows: 'formed from the ground' covers the birds too.
Rashi: the phrase is 'parsed apart': every living creature that the man called, that is its name forever. The English follows this: 'whatever the human called each living creature, that is its name'.

Ibn Ezra: the lamed of 'asher yiqra lo' carries the next word with it, so the sense is 'whatever the man calls [to] a living creature'. The second lamed is an explanatory addition. The English 'called each living creature' follows.

Radak (not normative): 'vayyetzer' is a pluperfect, 'had already formed' (וּכְבָר יָצַר): the animals were formed before the human, and here they are brought to him. Recorded; the English keeps the simple past.

Sforno (not normative): 'to see what he would call it' means that the human looks and considers which name suits each creature by the particular form it was given. The English 'to see what he would call it' follows.

apparatus: Radak's pluperfect 'had already formed' (וּכְבָר יָצַר) is recorded and not adopted.
The suffix ־לוֹ (2:19.19, 2:19.23) is masculine singular; the English 'it' refers to each creature in turn.

segments.english: The human gave names to all the livestock and to the birds of the sky and to every wild animal of the field; but for himself the human found no helper corresponding to him.
segments.literal: and-named the-human names to-all the-livestock and-to birds-of the-sky and-to-all wild-animals-of the-field; and-to man (= himself) not found a-helper like-in-front-of-him

tokens.note: wayyiqtol: 'call' with the object 'names' means 'give names'
The entry lists only sense 3, 'wild beasts', which does not fit the domestic animals in view (Ramban: ox, cow, goat, sheep). No sense is given for this token.
לְאָדָם with no article is not the name Adam here. Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Radak all read 'for himself' (לנפשו, לעצמו).

phrases.literal: 'and-named the-human names': 'call' with 'names' as object means 'give names'
'to-all the-livestock'

phrases.english: and to the birds of the sky
phrases.literal: 'and-to birds-of the-sky'

phrases.english: and to every wild animal of the field
phrases.literal: 'and-to-all wild-animals-of the-field'

phrases.english: but for himself the human found no helper corresponding to him
phrases.literal: 'and-to man (= himself) not found a-helper like-in-front-of-him'

grammar: וַיִּקְרָא ... שֵׁמוֹת: the verb קָרָא with the object 'names' means 'give names'.

Three phrases with ל ('to all the livestock', 'to the birds', 'to every wild animal') name the three classes. Ibn Ezra reads the first lamed as carrying through the list, and the English repeats 'to' for each.
וּלְאָדָם לֹא מָצָא: 'to himself he found no ...'. The reading 'for himself' follows Rashi and Ibn Ezra.
The zaqef gadol on וּלְאָדָם (2:20.11) divides the verse into the naming and the lack.
כְּנֶגְדּוֹ repeats 2:18.12. The English repeats 'corresponding to him' so that the search for a helper echoes the LORD's resolve.
segments.note: The sense of 'livestock' (2:20.5): the entry lists only 'wild beasts' (3), which does not fit the domestic animals meant. No sense is given for the token; the gloss is the English reading.

commentary.summary: Rashi: when the animals were brought in male and female, Adam said: 'Every one has a mate, and I have none'; at once the LORD God caused the deep sleep to fall on him. The English 'for himself' follows Rashi's 'for me'.
Ibn Ezra: 'lekhol ha-behemah' also carries the next item with it: 'to all the livestock' extends to 'and to the birds of the sky'. The English repeats 'to' for each item.
Ibn Ezra: 'ulʾadam lo matsa' means 'and for himself he did not find' (ולנפשו לא מצא), the same usage as in 1 Sam 12:11. The English 'for himself' follows.

apparatus: לְאָדָם (2:20.11): here the bare form is not the name Adam. Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Radak all read 'for himself'; the decision's name rule (4:25, 5:1–5) does not apply.

segments.english: The LORD God caused a deep sleep to fall upon the human, and he slept; then the LORD God took one of his sides and closed up the flesh in its place.
segments.literal: caused-to-fall the-LORD God a-deep-sleep upon the-human, and-slept; and-took one from-his-sides and-closed flesh in-its-place

tokens.note: hifil of נָפַל. Ibn Ezra: the heavier, added binyan
Ibn Ezra and Radak: tardemah is deeper than sleep (shenah). The entry lists no senses, so none is given.
wayyiqtol; the subject is the human
the subject shifts to the LORD God, who takes and closes
צֵלָע: 'side' (Rashi, Ibn Ezra); 'rib' in Onkelos and the literal reading (apparatus). The entry lists no senses.
closed up, of the wound
תַּחְתֶּנָּה: 'its place' (Ibn Ezra); the -nah ending is the feminine suffix for 'side'

phrases.english: the LORD God caused a deep sleep to fall
phrases.literal: 'caused-to-fall the-LORD God a-deep-sleep': the hifil with the verb first
'upon the-human'
'and-slept'
'and-took one from-his-sides': the subject is the LORD God

phrases.english: closed up the flesh in its place
phrases.literal: 'and-closed flesh in-its-place'

grammar: וַיַּפֵּל: the hifil 'caused to fall', with 'deep sleep' as the object. Ibn Ezra explains the stem as the heavier, added binyan.
The wayyiqtol chain changes subject. 'And he slept' is the human; 'and took' and 'and closed' have the LORD God as subject. The English marks the change with 'then the LORD God'.
אַחַת מִצַּלְעֹתָיו: 'one of his sides', with the numeral used partitively and a feminine noun for 'side'.
The etnaḥta on וַיִּישָׁן (2:21.7) divides the verse: the sleep first, then the taking and closing.
תַּחְתֶּנָּה: the feminine suffix -nah on the noun 'under' gives 'in its place'.
segments.note: 'One of his sides' follows Rashi and Ibn Ezra. 'Rib' is the lexicon's first gloss and Onkelos's reading, so the apparatus keeps it.

commentary.summary: Rashi: 'from his sides' means from his two sides (מִסְּטָרָיו), as the side of the Tabernacle (Exod 26). This is the reading of 'two faces' (Eruvin 18a). The English 'one of his sides' follows.
Rashi: 'vayisgor' is the place of the cut (מְקוֹם הַחֲתָךְ). The English 'closed up the flesh in its place' follows.
Rashi: the sleep is so that the man does not see the piece of flesh from which the woman is made and be shamed. The English keeps the order: he slept; then the LORD God took.
Ibn Ezra: 'vayappel' is from the heavier added binyan, the hifil: 'caused to fall'. The English follows.
Ibn Ezra: tardemah is more than sleep, and sleep is more than tenumah (slumber); the tav is added. The English 'a deep sleep' follows.
Ibn Ezra: 'achat mi-tsalotav' means one of two sides, as in 'the second side of the Tabernacle' (Exod 26:20); tsela is feminine and means 'side'. The English 'one of his sides' follows.
Ibn Ezra: tachtenah means 'its place' (מְקוֹמָהּ), singular; the nun is added. The English 'in its place' follows.
Radak (not normative) gives two readings: the side as two faces joined back to back, or tsela in its literal sense, 'rib', as Onkelos has it (עַלְעָא). Recorded; the English says 'sides', not 'ribs'.

apparatus: צֵלָע (2:21.10, 2:22.5): 'rib' in Onkelos (עַלְעָא) and in the literal sense; 'side' per Rashi and Ibn Ezra, which the English follows.

segments.english: The LORD God built the side which he had taken from the human into a woman, and brought her to the human.
segments.literal: and-built the-LORD God [obj] the-side which-had-taken from-the-human into-woman, and-brought-her to the-human

tokens.note: Rashi: built like a structure, wide below and narrow above, to hold the child like a granary of wheat. Ibn Ezra: the form may be from the heavy or the light binyan.
the object marker אֵת, with no English counterpart
the same word as 2:21.10. 'Side' per Rashi and Ibn Ezra.
relative particle
qatal in a relative clause: the taking precedes the building. The subject is the LORD God.
לְ + אִשָּׁה: 'to be a woman'. Rashi: 'to be', as 'and Gideon made it an ephod' (Judg 8:27).
hifil with the feminine suffix -ah, 'her'

phrases.literal: 'and-built the-LORD God': the verb comes first

phrases.english: the side which he had taken from the human
phrases.literal: '[obj] the-side which-had-taken from-the-human': the relative clause; 'he' is the LORD God
'into-woman': 'to be a woman' (Rashi)

phrases.english: and brought her to the human
phrases.literal: 'and-brought-her to the-human'

grammar: וַיִּבֶן ... אֶת־הַצֵּלָע: the verb 'build' with the definite object, marked by אֵת.
אֲשֶׁר־לָקַח: a relative clause with a qatal, so the taking comes before the building: 'which he had taken'.
לְאִשָּׁה: 'into a woman'. Rashi reads it as 'to be a woman', the result of the building.
וַיְבִאֶהָ: the hifil with the feminine suffix -ah takes the woman as object.
The etnaḥta on לְאִשָּׁה (2:22.10) divides the verse into the building and the bringing. The word אִשָּׁה here prepares the wordplay of 2:23.
segments.note: The woman is built from the side and is not called by a name in this unit.

commentary.summary: Rashi: 'vayiven' is like a building (kevinyan), wide below and narrow above, to hold the child like a granary of wheat so its weight does not press on the walls. The English keeps the verb 'built' and does not render the shape.
Rashi: 'built the side into a woman' means to be a woman, as 'and Gideon made it an ephod' (Judg 8:27) means to be an ephod. The English 'into a woman' follows.
Ibn Ezra: 'vayiven' may be from the heavy binyan or from the light, as in 'vayiqen' (Gen 33:19). The English reads the plain 'built'.

Ibn Ezra gives two readings of 'vayvi'ehah'. Either the verb describes Adam's thought on waking, that she was brought to him as the beasts were; or she was built outside the garden and then brought in, and when he looked he knew she had been taken from him. The English gives the bringing as plain narration; the first reading is recorded in the apparatus.

apparatus: 2:22.5 (הַצֵּלָע): 'rib' in Onkelos and in the literal sense; see 2:21.
2:22.11 (וַיְבִאֶהָ): Ibn Ezra's first reading, that the bringing is what Adam thought on waking, is recorded and not adopted.

segments.english: The human said: 'This time it is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh; for this reason she shall be called woman, because she was taken from man.'
segments.literal: and-said the-human: this time bone-of my-bones and-flesh-of my-flesh; for-this-reason she-shall-be-called woman, because from-man she-was-taken this-one

tokens.note: wayyiqtol: the verb comes first
demonstrative with 'time'
הַפַּעַם: 'this time'. Rashi: this time, unlike the beasts with whom Adam was not satisfied (Yevamot 63a).
the entry lists no senses
construct with the suffix; 'bone of my bones'
לְזֹאת: Ibn Ezra, 'because of this' (בעבור זאת)
niphal yiqtol. Ibn Ezra: yiqare means 'be called by the name of'.
אִשָּׁה is derived from אִישׁ (man): the yod of ish is absorbed by the dagesh of the shin (Radak). The English 'woman' from 'man' keeps the pair; the sound play is lost.
conjunction
מֵאִישׁ: 'from the man (male)'. The entry lists no senses.
pual perfect: passive
זֹאת used as a pronoun: 'this one', 'she'

phrases.literal: 'and-said the-human': the verb comes first
'this time': Rashi reads 'this time' as a contrast with the beasts
'bone of-my-bones'
'and-flesh of-my-flesh'

phrases.english: for this reason she shall be called woman
phrases.literal: 'for-this she-shall-be-called woman'

phrases.english: because she was taken from man
phrases.literal: 'because from-man she-was-taken this-one': the English puts 'she' before 'was taken'

grammar: זֹאת הַפַּעַם: 'this time', a demonstrative with a noun; it is a time marker and carries a contrast in Rashi.
עֶצֶם מֵעֲצָמַי וּבָשָׂר מִבְּשָׂרִי: the phrase 'bone of my bones' and 'flesh of my flesh' with the preposition מִן. The English adds 'it is' as a copula.
לְזֹאת יִקָּרֵא אִשָּׁה: the niphal 'shall be called', with לְ 'for this'. The pun ish/ishah is lost in English, but 'woman' and 'man' keep the derivation.
כִּי מֵאִישׁ לֻקְחָה־זֹּאת: the explanatory כִּי, 'because', and the pual 'was taken'. The closing demonstrative זֹאת is 'she'.
The verse is one speech by the human. The English keeps the speech in quotation marks, as the narrator's report of Adam's words.
segments.note: 'Woman' and 'man' stand for אִשָּׁה and אִישׁ. The English keeps the pair, which is the point of the derivation; the Hebrew sound play is not reproduced.

commentary.summary: Rashi: 'this time' teaches that Adam had relations with every beast and animal and was not satisfied with them (Yevamot 63a). The English 'This time' keeps the contrast open.
Rashi: 'language falls upon language': the world was created in the holy tongue, and the name 'woman' comes from 'man'. The English keeps the derivation in 'woman' and 'taken from man'.
Ibn Ezra: 'then he said: this time I have found a helper corresponding to me, for she came from me'. He marks the Lilith tale as a derash, not the plain sense. The English follows the plain sense.
Ibn Ezra: לְזֹאת means 'because of this', as in 'say you, she is my sister' (Gen 20:13). The English 'for this reason' follows.
Ibn Ezra on the morphology: the dagesh in the shin of ishah stands for the elided yod of ish. The dagesh keeps ishah from being confused with ishah, 'her husband'. It does not bear on the English.
Ibn Ezra: yiqare means 'is called upon the name of', so the naming is by a name. The English 'shall be called woman' follows.

apparatus: 2:23.14 (לֻקְחָה): the WLC reads לֻֽקֳחָה; the base text is לֻֽקְחָה.
2:23.4 (הַפַּעַם): 'this time' as Rashi's contrast with the beasts, and as plain 'at last', are both possible; the English keeps 'This time'.
2:23.11, 2:23.13 (אִשָּׁה, אִישׁ): the English 'woman' and 'man' keep the pair, not the Hebrew sound play.

grammar: עַל־כֵּן: the idiom 'therefore'. Rashi takes the words as the Holy Spirit's, a prohibition of forbidden unions for the sons of Noah (Sanhedrin 57b). The English keeps them as the narrator's comment, not as Adam's speech.
יַעֲזָב ... וְדָבַק ... וְהָיוּ: the yiqtol gives a general statement, the weqatal of 'and clings' continues it, and the plural 'they shall be' has the pair as subject.
אֶת־אָבִיו וְאֶת־אִמּוֹ: the object marker is repeated with each noun, so the English 'his father and his mother' gives both objects.
לִבְשָׂר אֶחָד: the preposition ל before a noun marks the predicate: 'one flesh'.
The zaqef qaton on אִישׁ (2:24.4) and on בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ (2:24.10) divides the verse into three clauses: leave, cling, be one flesh.
segments.note: The English keeps 'one flesh' open between union and offspring. Rashi's reading (the child) is recorded, and so is Ibn Ezra's reading ('as if they are one'), which the English follows.

commentary.summary: Rashi: 'therefore' is the Holy Spirit's word, forbidding forbidden unions to the sons of Noah (Sanhedrin 57b). The English keeps 'therefore' as the narrator's comment, not as Adam's speech.

Ibn Ezra, on 2:24.11–13 (filed at 2:24): 'they shall be one flesh' means 'as if they are' (כאלו הם), or that they shall resemble what they were. Some say it means another offspring, which he calls far. The English 'they shall be one flesh' follows the first reading; the others are in the apparatus.
Rashi: the child is formed by the two of them, and there their flesh becomes one. The English keeps 'one flesh' open and does not narrow it to the child; this reading is recorded here.

Ramban (not normative): the child reading is not enough, since animals also become one flesh in their young. The sense is that the wife is as near as his own flesh, and he desires that she be always with him. Recorded; not adopted.

apparatus: לִבְשָׂר אֶחָד (2:24.12–13): Rashi's reading (the child) and Ibn Ezra's ('as if they are one', 2:23 apparatus) are both recorded. The English keeps the phrase.
